text:
Data Ingest and Acquisition

#' Acquire Netflix What We Watched Reports
#' 
#' This function will acquire and standardize all data for MP#01
#' from Netflix. Because Netflix hosts the data files behind a CDN, we
#' are accessing the release pages and automatically extracting links to the
#' relevant files (with CDN hash). 
#' 
#' After import, files are stacked vertically and some basic cleaning is
#' performed. 
load_netflix_data <- function(){
  # Note to students: Make sure you have installed the tidyverse and fs packages
  #                   before beginning this assignment. If you aren't sure,
  #                   simply run `library(tidyverse)` at your R Console and, if
  #                   you don't see an error message, `tidyverse` has been 
  #                   installed. (Same for `fs`) If you still need to install
  #                   either package, use the `install.packages` function as 
  #                   demonstrated in class.
  library(tidyverse)
  library(rvest)
  library(readxl)
  library(fs)
  
  data_dir <- path("data", "mp01")
    
  if(!dir_exists(data_dir)){
    dir_create(data_dir, showWarnings=FALSE, recurse=TRUE)
  }
  
  NETFLIX_URLS <- list(
    `2023H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-a-netflix-engagement-report",
    `2023H2` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-second-half-of-2023",
    `2024H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-first-half-of-2024",
    `2024H2` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-second-half-of-2024",
    `2025H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-first-half-of-2025",
    `2025H2` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-second-half-of-2025",
    `2026H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-first-half-of-2026"
  )
  
  download_if_needed <- function(url, local){
    if(!file_exists(local)){
      download.file(url, local, quiet = TRUE, mode = "wb")
    }
    
    return(local)
  }
    
  NETFLIX_URLS |> 
    map(read_html) |> 
    map(html_element, xpath = "//a[contains(@href, '.xlsx')]") |> 
    map_chr(html_attr, "href") |> 
    enframe("period", "url") |> 
   mutate(path = path(data_dir, paste0(period, ".xlsx")), 
          path = map2(url, path, download_if_needed), 
          data = map(path, read_excel, skip=3, na="*"), 
          data = map(data, \(x) x |> mutate(`Release Date` = as.Date(`Release Date`)))) |>
    unnest(data) |> 
    select(-url, -path) |> 
    mutate(year=str_sub(period, 1, 4), 
           half=str_sub(period, start=6), 
           period_start = make_date(year, if_else(half==1, 1, 7), 1), 
           period_end = make_date(year, if_else(half==1, 6, 12), if_else(half==1, 30, 31))) |> 
    filter(!is.na(`Hours Viewed`)) |> 
    mutate(live_event = !is.na(Runtime) & str_detect(Runtime, "\\d+:\\d+\\*"), 
           clean_time = str_remove(Runtime, fixed("*")),
           Runtime = 60 * hour(hm(clean_time)) + minute(hm(clean_time))) |>
    select(-clean_time) |>
    mutate(Runtime = coalesce(Runtime, mean(Runtime, na.rm=TRUE)), 
           .by=Title, 
           Title = stringi::stri_trans_general(Title, "Latin-ASCII"),
           Title = str_remove(Title, " // .*"), 
           Title = str_remove(Title, "[^[:ascii:]].*"), 
           Title = str_trim(Title)) |>
    filter_out(Title == "") |>
    select(year, 
           period, 
           period_start, 
           period_end, 
           Title, 
           -half, 
           Runtime, 
           Views, 
           `Hours Viewed`, 
           `Release Date`,
           `Available Globally?`, 
           live_event)
}
## Data Cleaning and Preparation

###It is convenient to highlight the fact that Netflix is not consistent with some of the data presented. The tittles of the shows or movies are not standardized; for example, we can find Seinfeld: Season 1 and Seinfeld: Season 3, but Stranger Things and Stranger Things 3. Similarly, for Runtime, some catalog entries do not have a published run time. For the total hours a title was viewed, shows with low hours (less than 50,000 hours of view time) are omitted.

section: Task 6: Advanced Exploratory Analysis including tables
text:
Task 6: Advanced Exploratory Analysis including tables
As our analytical scope expands to multi-variable queries, standalone data points are insufficient. We will use tables to deliver publication-quality insights to Netflix senior leadership.

Top-Performing Content by Period and Market Share
To isolate what drives peak platform engagement, we mapped the single highest-performing title within each six-month window. Furthermore, we calculated that title’s “market share”—the exact fraction of total platform viewing hours it captured during that specific period.

title: STA 9750 Submission Material
section: Exploratory Questions -Table Answers. Here we employ the {gt} package to construct structured, presentation-ready tables that surface deep performance trends across reporting periods.
text:
Exploratory Questions -Table Answers. Here we employ the {gt} package to construct structured, presentation-ready tables that surface deep performance trends across reporting periods.
For a simpler overview of the different titles and the amount of total hours they were viewed, we will expand on the top title per period and the fraction of total viewership it captured. Therefore, we mapped the highest performing title withing each half or six-month period.

library(tidyverse)
library(gt)

# Step 1: Calculate total viewership hours for each period to use as a baseline denominator
period_totals = NETFLIX_DATA |>
  group_by(period) |>
  summarise(total_period_hours = sum(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE))

# Step 2: Find the top title per period and join the totals to calculate the fraction
top_titles_table = NETFLIX_DATA |>
  group_by(period, title) |>
  summarise(title_hours = sum(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  group_by(period) |>
  slice_max(title_hours, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  left_join(period_totals, by = "period") |>
  mutate(viewership_fraction = title_hours / total_period_hours) |>
  ungroup()

# Step 3: Format the summary data into an executive-ready gt table
top_titles_table |>
  select(period, title, title_hours, viewership_fraction) |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Top Title in Each Period",
    subtitle = "Analysis of leading titles and global viewership share"
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    period = "Reporting Period",
    title = "Top Performing Title",
    title_hours = "Total Hours Viewed",
    viewership_fraction = "Platform Share (%)"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = title_hours,
    decimals = 0,
    suffixing = TRUE # to change large numbers to M (Millions) or B (Billions)
  ) |>
  fmt_percent(
    columns = viewership_fraction,
    decimals = 2
  ) |>
  tab_options(
    table.width = pct(100),
    heading.background.color = "#98FF98" # Choosing an easy-on-the-eye color
  )

Multi-season series or shows: Most of the attention among viewers on Netflix fall into this category. There are thousands of titles gaining Over 0.9% to 1.35% of total platform attention.
Viewership concentration: Although some titles vanish after certain period due to audience decrease, the percentage of watch time capture by the top shows remains stable from period to period. This situation could indicate that new releases are needed to keep this trends.


library(tidyverse)

# Step 1: Calculate total titles and hours per period, split by global availability
catalog_growth <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  group_by(period, available_globally) |>
  summarise(
    title_count = n_distinct(title),

text:
To evaluate how Netflix’s catalog changed in size over the periods, we have risen the attention over Regionally Restricted and Globally Available content and their total run-time over every period. Looking at the data presented in the table above, there is an undisputed disproportion in share of viewer attention. Regional Restricted content has the major number of titles, but Globally Available captures by far the majority of the watching hours spent.

library(tidyverse) 
library(gt) 
# Step 1: Calculate consistency metrics for every title across all periods 
comfort_food_analysis = NETFLIX_DATA |> 
  group_by(title) |> 
  summarise( 
    periods_tracked = n_distinct(period), # Must be present across reporting cycles 
    average_hours = mean(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE), 
    minimum_hours = min(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE),
    viewership_stability = sd(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE), # Low SD = stable viewership 
    .groups = "drop" ) |> 
  # Filter for true staples: must appear in at least 6 periods and maintain high baseline views 
  filter(periods_tracked >= 6, minimum_hours > 1000000) |>
  slice_max(minimum_hours, n = 10, with_ties = FALSE) # Grab the top 10 most reliable anchors 

# Step 2: Shortcuts for report
top_staple_name = comfort_food_analysis$title[1]
top_staple_floor = round(comfort_food_analysis$minimum_hours[1] / 1e6,1)

# Step 3. Render the true Question 3 executive table
comfort_food_analysis |> 
  select(title, periods_tracked, average_hours, minimum_hours) |> 
  gt() |> 
  tab_header( 
    title = "Platform Content Anchors and Comfort Food Staples",
    subtitle = "Top 10 titles with the highest guaranteed baseline views across tracking periods" 
  ) |> 
  cols_label( 
    title = "Content Title", 
    periods_tracked = "Periods Active", 
    average_hours = "Average Hours / Period", 
    minimum_hours = "Floor Viewership or Worst Period" 
  ) |> 
  
  fmt_number( 
    columns = c(average_hours, minimum_hours), 
    decimals = 0, 
    suffixing = TRUE 
  ) |> 
  
  tab_options( 
    table.width = pct(100), 
    heading.background.color = "#005B60"

# Step 1. Applying the 4-hour runtime benchmark to classify content categories
classified_catalog = NETFLIX_DATA |>

library(tidyverse)
library(gt)

# Step 1. Establish title key words to classify Live and pre-taped content 
live_classification = "Live|Roast of|WWE Raw|Awards|Comedy Special|The Roast"

classified_live_data = NETFLIX_DATA |>
  mutate(
    is_live = str_detect(title, regex(live_classification, ignore_case = TRUE)),
    content_format = if_else(is_live, "Live Event / Special", "Pre-taped Content")
  )

#Step 2. Aggregate counts and comparison

live_vs_taped_summary = classified_live_data |>
  group_by(content_format) |>
  summarise(
    total_titles = n_distinct(title),
    average_views = mean(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE),

title: STA 9750 Submission Material
text:
Corporate Strategy memo
TO: Netflix Senior Leadership & Executive Committee
FROM: Carolina Lenes Arreola DATE: October 12, 2026
SUBJECT: Data-driven portfolio optimization for Netflix’s original content strategy for 2027 and beyond.

Executive Summary
To optimized resource allocation, maximize profitability, and improve platform performance metrics, this brief report evaluates the core data features that drive Netflix content environment. These features include: viewership patterns, program titles, runtimes, the total hours consumed, the original release windows, global distribution rights, and live or pre-recorded content. This memo focuses in four Strategic Dimensions: Format Segmentation (Series vs. Movies), Catalog Architecture and Licensing Evolution (Regionally licensed and Globally available content), Platform Content Anchors and Comfort Food Staples, and Platform Analytics: Live Events vs. Pre-Taped Content.


Portfolio overview (Data insights)
It is important to highlight that the data used for this memo-report was acquired from Netflix’s corporate relations website and it includes the “What We Watched” reports; the catalog span a chronological footprint, capturing active consumer content entries tracking from 2010-04-01 up to modern releases observed in 2026-06-29. Within this timeline, NETFLIX tracks give us a total of 24427 unique titles.


Strategic Dimensions 1: Format Segmentation (Series vs. Movies)
By deploying a four-hour runtime classification benchmark to distinguish multi-episode serialized season blocks from standalone features (movies). Viewers are concentrating their attention on TV Shows blocks. Across every tracked reporting interval, seasonal TV Show blocks consistently command an average of 90% of global platform viewing hours. Conversely, traditional standalone movies carry a mere 10% share of the platform consumption time.
To optimize structural content expenditures, Netflix builds its infrastructure on global subscribers who prefer episodic or seasonal content. My recommendation falls on focusing production budget on series or seasonal content over movies.


Strategic Dimension 2: Catalog Architecture and Licensing Evolution (Regionally licensed and Globally available content).
From the distribution and licensing point of view, the majority of platform content goes to Regionally Restricted content, leaving only 35.1% of all catalog titles identified as globally available content. However, when this distribution is weighted by the actual engagement, titles with global viewers lead with 51.9% of all hours viewed on the platform. So, per asset or show, universally available content generates a significant higher engagement.
Tracking total volume and viewership across global rights segments, it is evident that globally accessible content generates more significant engagement; therefore, it is recommended to focus on low-cost regionally licensed content while increasing investment on assets that secure universally available distribution rights.


Strategic Dimension 3: Platform Content Anchors and Comfort Food Staples.
Data shows that long-term subscriber retention is fundamentally anchored by evergreen “comfort food staples.” Those shows can also serve as a hook for new subscribers. Massive audience are concentrated on top titles like True Beauty: Limited Series which floor or worst scenario of views ranked the 132.2 million hours. These assets maintain high historical longevity of the platform content.
My recommendation is to secure or renew the licensing agreements for these content anchors and comfort food staples. That can keep subscribers retention and new subscription increases.


Strategic Dimension 4: Platform Analytics: Live Events vs. Pre-Taped Content
While pre-recorded content takes the lead in the platform’s content infrastructure at 76.3 % of total engagement hours, real-time Live Infrastructure investments like comedy roasts, awards, and sport shows are an exceptional engagement hook, securing 23.7% share.
Although pre-recorded content amounting to a big staggering 24237 of the total titles and which viewership peak reaches r pre_taped_peak_millions million hours, live specials represent 190 of the total titles and sum r live_peak_millions million hours in its viewership peak. Live content consolidates massive audience volumes into single, real-time windows.
My recommendation is to increase the budget allocation for live-events format specials in order to increase real-time platform engagement.


Actionable Blueprint for 2027 Capital Allocation
In sum, to safeguard Netflix’s global objectives, I recommend to prioritize the allocation of resources for your 2027 and beyond budget on the following content:

Episodic or seasonal content over standardalones.

Globally available content over Regionally Registered content.
Anchors and comfort food staples securing renewals and new subscriptions.
Live Events to consolidate live engagement increases.

Please let me know if you would like to set up a meeting to present and discuss the findings in this data analysis.
Sincerely,
Carolina Lenes Arreola Data Analyst

title: Data Ingest and Acquisition
text:
Data Cleaning and Preparation
It is convenient to highlight the fact that Netflix is not consistent with some of the data presented. The tittles of the shows or movies are not standardized; for example, we can find Seinfeld: Season 1 and Seinfeld: Season 3, but Stranger Things and Stranger Things 3. Similarly, for Runtime, some catalog entries do not have a published run time. For the total hours a title was viewed, shows with low hours (less than 50,000 hours of view time) are omitted.
So, we have renamed some columns, modified date format, and created new columns to better manage the data for our analysis.

title: Data Ingest and Acquisition
text:
Exploratory information

Range
The data analyzed is concentrated in a period covering the dates of releases, we used the min() and max() built-in-functions to determine its range.
The range of the data goes from 2010-04-01 to 2026-06-29.


Shows and movies covered
Among that range and after reviewing the different unique titles, we found a total of 24427 in the NETFLIX report.


The Bridgerton universe
Out of the total unique titles, one in particular have a universe of content itself. Although it is not a top title for anchors and comfort food content, viewers have spent 4862.8 hours watching shows from the Bridgerton universe.


Stranger Things
Another title that calls our attention is the show Stranger Things which has 5 seasons. We analyzed how many hours viewers spent watching it. For this purpose we left out titles from companion promotional media like Beyond Stranger Things, Tales from ’85, and Stranger Things: Fireplace.
Our exploration delivered a staggering 5588.9 million total hours to the 5-season series.


Audience concentration
We wanted to know what people watch the most, so we focused our attention to the Top 10 titles of the first half of 2026 (2026H1).
Our conclusion points out that viewers dedicate 6.7% of the total watch time across all the platform.


Universal distribution
Viewers have different preferences; in NETFLIX catalog, global availability of a show or movie makes a significant difference.
When analizing the volume of listings , 35.1% of all catalog titles are identified as globally available. Nevertheless, when we weight this distribution by the actual engagement, titles with global viewers lead with a 51.9% of all hours viewed on the platform. So, per asset or show, universally available content generates a significant higher engagement.

title: Data Ingest and Acquisition
text:
Advanced Exploratory Analysis including tables
As our scope expands to multi-variable queries, standalone data points are insufficient. We will use tables to deliver publication-quality insights, which includes: 1. Top-Performing Content by Period and Market Share, 2. How Netflix’s catalog have changed in size over the periods, 3. Titles have had the most consistently high viewership across all periods (“comfort food” content), 4. Fraction of time spent on ‘shows’ vs movies, 5. Performance of live events compare to pre-taped content.

1. Top-Performing Content by Period and Market Share.
For a simpler overview of the different titles and the amount of total hours they were viewed, we will expand on the top title per period and the fraction of total viewership it captured. To isolate what drives peak platform engagement, we mapped the single highest-performing title within each six-month window.
Furthermore, we calculated that title’s “market share”—the exact fraction of total platform viewing hours it captured during that specific period.

library(tidyverse)
library(gt)

# Step 1: Calculate total viewership hours for each period to use as a baseline denominator
period_totals = NETFLIX_DATA |>
  group_by(period) |>
  summarise(total_period_hours = sum(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE))

# Step 2: Find the top title per period and join the totals to calculate the fraction
top_titles_table = NETFLIX_DATA |>
  group_by(period, title) |>
  summarise(title_hours = sum(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  group_by(period) |>
  slice_max(title_hours, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  left_join(period_totals, by = "period") |>
  mutate(viewership_fraction = title_hours / total_period_hours) |>
  ungroup()

# Step 3: Format the summary data into an executive-ready gt table
top_titles_table |>
  select(period, title, title_hours, viewership_fraction) |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(

    subtitle = "Analysis of leading titles and global viewership share"

  cols_label(

    decimals = 0,

My recommendation is to secure or renew the licensing agreements for these content anchors and comfort food staples. That can keep subscribers retention and new subscription increases.


Strategic Dimension 4: Platform Analytics: Live Events vs. Pre-Taped Content
While pre-recorded content takes the lead in the platform’s content infrastructure at 76.3 % of total engagement hours, real-time Live Infrastructure investments like comedy roasts, awards, and sport shows are an exceptional engagement hook, securing 23.7% share.
Although pre-recorded content amounting to a big staggering 24237 of the total titles and which viewership peak reaches 964.1 million hours, live specials represent 190 of the total titles and sum 68.7 million hours in its viewership peak. Live content consolidates massive audience volumes into single, real-time windows.
My recommendation is to increase the budget allocation for live-events format specials in order to increase real-time platform engagement.


Actionable Blueprint for 2027 Capital Allocation
In sum, to safeguard Netflix’s global objectives, I recommend to prioritize the allocation of resources for your 2027 and beyond budget on the following content:

Episodic or seasonal content over standardalones.

Globally available content over Regionally Registered content.
Anchors and comfort food staples securing renewals and new subscriptions.
Live Events to consolidate live engagement increases.

title: Data Ingest and Acquisition
text:
Advanced Exploratory Analysis including tables
As our scope expands to multi-variable queries, standalone data points are insufficient. We will use tables to deliver publication-quality insights, which includes: 1. Top-Performing Content by Period and Market Share, 2. How Netflix’s catalog have changed in size over the periods, 3. Titles have had the most consistently high viewership across all periods (“comfort food” content), 4. Fraction of time spent on ‘shows’ vs movies, 5. Performance of live events compare to pre-taped content.

1. Top-Performing Content by Period and Market Share.
For a simpler overview of the different titles and the amount of total hours they were viewed, we will expand on the top title per period and the fraction of total viewership it captured. To isolate what drives peak platform engagement, we mapped the single highest-performing title within each six-month window.
Furthermore, we calculated that title’s “market share”—the exact fraction of total platform viewing hours it captured during that specific period.

library(tidyverse)
library(gt)

# Step 1: Calculate total viewership hours for each period to use as a baseline denominator
period_totals = NETFLIX_DATA |>
  group_by(period) |>
  summarise(total_period_hours = sum(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE))

# Step 2: Find the top title per period and join the totals to calculate the fraction
top_titles_table = NETFLIX_DATA |>
  group_by(period, title) |>
  summarise(title_hours = sum(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  group_by(period) |>
  slice_max(title_hours, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  left_join(period_totals, by = "period") |>
  mutate(viewership_fraction = title_hours / total_period_hours) |>
  ungroup()

# Step 3: Format the summary data into an executive-ready gt table
top_titles_table |>
  select(period, title, title_hours, viewership_fraction) |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Top Title in Each Period",
    subtitle = "Analysis of leading titles and global viewership share"
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    period = "Reporting Period",
    title = "Top Performing Title",
    title_hours = "Total Hours Viewed",
    viewership_fraction = "Platform Share (%)"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = title_hours,
    decimals = 0,
    suffixing = TRUE # to change large numbers to M (Millions) or B (Billions)
  ) |>
  fmt_percent(
    columns = viewership_fraction,
    decimals = 2
  ) |>
  tab_options(
    table.width = pct(100),
    heading.background.color = "#98FF98" # Choosing an easy-on-the-eye color
  )

2. How Netflix’s catalog have changed in size over the periods.
To evaluate how Netflix’s catalog changed in size over the periods, we have risen the attention over Regionally Restricted and Globally Available content and their total run-time over every period. On the table below, we will see that there is an undisputed disproportion in share of viewer attention.

3. Titles with the most consistently high viewership across all periods (“comfort food” content).
Data shows that long-term subscriber retention is fundamentally anchored by evergreen “comfort food staples,” as follows.

library(tidyverse) 
library(gt) 
# Step 1: Calculate consistency metrics for every title across all periods 
comfort_food_analysis = NETFLIX_DATA |> 
  group_by(title) |> 
  summarise( 
    periods_tracked = n_distinct(period), # Must be present across reporting cycles 
    average_hours = mean(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE), 
    minimum_hours = min(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE),
    viewership_stability = sd(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE), # Low SD = stable viewership 
    .groups = "drop" ) |> 
  # Filter for true staples: must appear in at least 6 periods and maintain high baseline views 
  filter(periods_tracked >= 6, minimum_hours > 1000000) |>
  slice_max(minimum_hours, n = 10, with_ties = FALSE) # Grab the top 10 most reliable anchors 

# Step 2: Shortcuts for report
top_staple_name = comfort_food_analysis$title[1]
top_staple_floor = round(comfort_food_analysis$minimum_hours[1] / 1e6,1)

# Step 3. Render the table
comfort_food_analysis |> 
  select(title, periods_tracked, average_hours, minimum_hours) |> 
  gt() |> 
  tab_header(

  ) |>

    periods_tracked = "Periods Active", 
    average_hours = "Average Hours / Period", 
    minimum_hours = "Floor Viewership or Worst Period" 
  ) |>

    decimals = 0, 
    suffixing = TRUE 
  ) |>

4. Fraction of time spent on ‘shows’ vs movies.
Following, we are going to observe how many hours viewers spend on series or shows and movies. We deployed a four-hour runtime classification benchmark to distinguish multi-episode serialized season blocks from standalone features (movies).

library(tidyverse)
library(gt)
# Step 1. Applying the 4-hour runtime benchmark to classify content categories
classified_catalog = NETFLIX_DATA |>
  filter(!is.na(run_time)) |> # To exclude any missing runtime data
  mutate(
    content_type = if_else(run_time > 240, "TV Show (Season Block)", "Movie / Standalone")
)
# Step 2. Compute aggregate period benchmarks and volume fractions
format_fractions = classified_catalog |>
  group_by(period, content_type) |>
  summarise(
    category_hours = sum(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop_last"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    total_period_hours = sum(category_hours),
    viewership_fraction = category_hours / total_period_hours
  ) |>
ungroup()

# Shortcuts for report (memo)

avg_movie_share = round(mean(format_fractions$viewership_fraction[format_fractions$content_type == "Movie / Standalone"]) * 100, 1)

avg_tv_share = 100 - avg_movie_share

# Step 3. Rendering a presentation table

format_fractions |>
  select(period, content_type, category_hours, viewership_fraction) |>
  gt(groupname_col = "period") |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Format Segmentation: TV Shows vs. Movies",
    subtitle = "Analysis of platform viewing distribution based on a 4-hour runtime classification benchmark"
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    content_type = "Content Format Classification",
    category_hours = "Total Hours Consumed",
    viewership_fraction = "Platform Engagement Share (%)"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = category_hours,
    decimals = 0,
    suffixing = TRUE
  ) |>
  fmt_percent(
    columns = viewership_fraction,
    decimals = 2
  ) |>
  tab_options(
    table.width = pct(100),
    heading.background.color = "#76C1B1"
  )

5. Performance of live events compare to pre-taped content.
As we will see in the table below, the amount of pre-recorded content surpasses live content. However, the engagement is contrary to the content allocation.

library(tidyverse)
library(gt)

# Step 1. Establish title key words to classify Live and pre-taped content 
live_classification = "Live|Roast of|WWE Raw|Awards|Comedy Special|The Roast"

classified_live_data = NETFLIX_DATA |>
  mutate(
    is_live = str_detect(title, regex(live_classification, ignore_case = TRUE)),
    content_format = if_else(is_live, "Live Event / Special", "Pre-taped Content")
  )

#Step 2. Aggregate counts and comparison

live_vs_taped_summary = classified_live_data |>
  group_by(content_format) |>
  summarise(
    total_titles = n_distinct(title),
    average_views = mean(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE),
    top_tier_views = max(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Step 3. Shortcuts for report (memo)
# Engagement
pct_live_hours = round((live_vs_taped_summary$average_views[live_vs_taped_summary$content_format == "Live Event / Special"] / sum(live_vs_taped_summary$average_views)) * 100, 1)

pct_taped_hours = round((live_vs_taped_summary$average_views[live_vs_taped_summary$content_format == "Pre-taped Content"] / sum(live_vs_taped_summary$average_views)) * 100, 1)

# Number of titles by type of content (pre-recorded vs live)
count_live_titles = live_vs_taped_summary$total_titles[live_vs_taped_summary$content_format == "Live Event / Special"] 
count_taped_titles = live_vs_taped_summary$total_titles[live_vs_taped_summary$content_format == "Pre-taped Content"]

live_peak_millions = round(live_vs_taped_summary$top_tier_views[live_vs_taped_summary$content_format == "Live Event / Special"] / 1e6, 1)
pre_taped_peak_millions = round(live_vs_taped_summary$top_tier_views[live_vs_taped_summary$content_format == "Pre-taped Content"] / 1e6, 1)

# Step 4. Format in gt for presentation or report
live_vs_taped_summary |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Platform Analytics: Live Events vs. Pre-Taped Content",
    subtitle = "Strategic comparison of baseline averages and top-tier performance"
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    content_format = "Content Type",
    total_titles = "Total Tracked Titles",
    average_views = "Average Viewership Hours",
    top_tier_views = "Top-Tier Viewership Peak"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = total_titles,
    decimals = 0
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(average_views, top_tier_views),
    decimals = 0,
    suffixing = TRUE
  ) |>
  tab_options(
    table.width = pct(100),
    heading.background.color = "#5A738E"
  )
